error.description:
Stable machine code, present on the responses that carry one — the widget's 401/403/404 and the
attachment 413. Optional because most errors here only have a message, but it has to be part of
the schema: tsoa emits `additionalProperties: false`, so an undeclared key makes every coded
response violate the shape its own spec tells a caller to parse.

OPTIONAL RATHER THAN A SEPARATE CODED-ERROR SCHEMA, and not for brevity: on the routes that
carry codes, the same status can arrive with and without one. A widget-config 404 is
`widget_unknown` when the widget id misses and a bare `Feedback portal not found` when the
portal id does; a widget-config 401 is `token_invalid` for a bad token and a bare
`Forbidden, there is no auth token` when the header is absent. A variant with `error` required
would be declared on exactly those routes and would be wrong half the time they fail.

Branch on it when it is there and fall back to the status when it is not. The vocabulary:
401 `token_expired` (fetch a new token and retry once) | `token_invalid` | `dev_key_invalid` |
`dev_origin_rejected`;
403 `widget_not_enabled` | `insufficient_scope` | `mcp_disabled_by_account` | `no_paid_seat`;
404 `widget_unknown` | `widget_deleted` | `widget_inactive` | `widget_no_categories`;
413 `file_too_large`.
The widget half of that list is the contract in docs/CRA-24100-widget-token-endpoint.md and is
pinned by widgetFailureTaxonomy.test.ts — change the three together.

Left as a free string rather than an enum on purpose — a closed set turns every new code into
a breaking change for a generated client, and new codes are the whole point of the field.

RetryableErrorResponse.description:
The 503 body — NOT `GeneralErrorResponse`, which it would violate.

`code` and `retryAfter` are contract terms (see `ServiceUnavailableError`), and the shared error
schema is `additionalProperties: false`, so a route declaring `GeneralErrorResponse` for its 503
documents a shape this service has never sent. Same defect CRA-24377 reported against the
widget 404, one status along.

`code` rather than `error` because that is what the handler has always emitted here and callers
branch on it; renaming it to match the 4xx family would be the breaking change.

code.description: Always `retryable`. What distinguishes a transient failure from the permanent 4xx ones.

owner.description:
Email address of the person who submitted the feedback.

Resolved against this portal, in order: an administrative user of the portal, then an
existing portal user with that address. If neither matches, a portal user IS CREATED for
the address — they hold no password and can never sign in, they simply exist so the
feedback is attributed to them and so their next submission resolves to the same person.
The new user is homed in `company` when you send one. Otherwise the company is inferred from
the address: an existing portal company whose people already use that email domain, else a new
company named for the domain. An address at a free-mail or disposable domain infers nothing —
`gmail.com` is not a customer — so those submitters go to the portal's "Individual Submitters"
company, which is created on first use and holds everyone whose company is not determinable.

Omit it and the feedback is attributed to the portal's anonymous submitter (the same as
sending `anonymous: true`).

This is NOT a user ID — sending anything that is not an email address returns
422 (`owner must be a valid email address`), like every other value error here.

widgetId.description:
The widget this submission came from — send it on every widget submission.

It names the configuration the form was rendered from, so the settings an administrator made
per widget are applied to the submission rather than having to be echoed back by the page. Today
that is the importance: a widget whose form does not ask (`hideImportance`) submits no
`importanceId`, and the widget's own `defaultImportanceId` is applied here instead of the
portal's default. Anything else that becomes per-widget will be applied the same way, with no
change needed in the page.

**A widget id this portal does not have is a 422 on an API key and is ignored on a widget
credential.** An administrator can delete a widget while a page is open, and a submission
somebody has already typed must not be lost to it — the portal's default applies, exactly as a
submission naming no widget would get. An API key can re-read and retry, so it is told.

Omit it and nothing per-widget is applied; the portal's own defaults stand. An explicit
`importanceId` always wins over the widget's.

importanceId.description:
Portal importance — numeric ID OR exact name (case-insensitive). When
omitted, the portal's `isDefault: true` importance is used (see
`GET /feedback_portal/{portalId}/importances`) — or, when `widgetId` names a widget that hides
the importance question, that widget's `defaultImportanceId`.

company.description:
Customer company — numeric ID OR exact name (case-insensitive). Resolve via
`GET /feedback_portal/{portalId}/companies`.

Sets the feedback's company, and is also the company a submitter created from `owner` is
placed in. A value that matches no company in this portal is a 422 listing the valid ones;
it is never created and never silently ignored.

Only settable on restricted portals — a public portal attributes everything to its default
company, so sending it there is a 422.

anonymous.description:
Submit without attributing the feedback to a person: the item is attributed to the portal's
anonymous submitter, so it reads as anonymous everywhere.

This is the explicit form of what omitting `owner` already does — send it when you want the
intent to be visible in the request rather than inferred from an absent field.

Mutually exclusive with `owner` — sending both returns 422. `company` is still
honoured, so anonymous feedback can still be grouped under a customer company.

submitterId.description:
Your own identifier for this submitter — **the primary identity key when you send it.**

Prefer it over relying on `owner` alone. Matching on your id rather than on an email address
is what makes one address belonging to several of your tenants resolve to several distinct
people instead of collapsing into one, and it survives the person changing their email.

Send it and `owner` together: the id is how the submitter is matched, and the address is how
they are notified, so `owner` is still required.

**Adding it later is safe.** If you have been submitting without it, the first submission that
carries an id is matched by `owner` and the id is adopted onto that existing person — your
submitters are upgraded, not duplicated. From then on the id is what identifies them.

At most 255 characters; longer returns 422 rather than being truncated, because a truncated
id would silently resolve to the wrong person. Compared exactly, including case.

issuer.description:
Which of your systems `submitterId` came from. Only meaningful alongside `submitterId`.

Send it when more than one of your systems posts to the same portal: user `42` in your billing
app is not user `42` in your analytics app, and without an issuer they would resolve to one
person. With one system you can omit it — it defaults to this portal.

The same value the browser/widget route carries as its token `iss` claim, so a submitter
resolves to the same person whichever route their feedback arrives on.

At most 255 characters; longer returns 422.

submitterName.description:
The submitter's name, as your own system holds it.

Send it and the portal shows a person. Omit it and the only name Craft can produce is the
local part of `owner`, so `jane.doe@acme.com` reads as "jane.doe" on every card and in every
digest.

**Refreshed on every submission that matches**, not only on the first one — the same as
`owner`. If the person is renamed in your system, the next submission carrying their
`submitterId` updates the stored name, so you never have to reconcile it separately.

One string, not first/last: it is split on the last space for storage and joined back for
display, so what you send is what the portal shows.

Requires pass-through identity on the portal, like `submitterId`, and requires `owner` — a
name with nobody to attach it to is a 422 rather than a value quietly dropped.

At most 256 characters; longer returns 422 rather than being truncated.

sourceUrl.description:
The page this feedback was submitted from — **including its query string.**

The query string is the point, not an incidental: a tenant, an account or a product area often
sits in a URL parameter, and a PM reading the feedback item needs the link that reproduces what
the submitter was looking at. Nothing is stripped, re-encoded or normalised.

In a single-page application send the URL **in view at submit**, not the one the page first
loaded with — they are usually different and only the first is useful.

Must be an absolute `http://` or `https://` URL of at most 2048 characters. Anything else
(a relative path, a `javascript:` or `data:` URL, surrounding whitespace, a NUL byte) returns
422 rather than being stored or quietly cleaned up.

Optional, and omitting it is the ordinary case for a backend integration that has no page.

attachmentIds.description:
Files to attach, as ids returned by `POST /feedback_portal/{portalId}/attachment`.

**Upload first, then submit.** The upload call stores the bytes against the portal and hands
back an id; naming that id here is what files it with this piece of feedback. That order is
what lets a form attach files while the submitter is still typing — there is no feedback item
to attach to until they press send — and it means a failed upload costs a retry rather than
the whole submission.

Each id must be one of **this** portal's own uploads and must not already be attached to
another feedback item; anything else is a 422. At most 10 per item. Unlike `metadata`, an id
that resolves to nothing is never quietly dropped — an attachment the submitter watched upload
must not vanish behind a 200.

is what makes one address belonging to several of your tenants resolve to several distinct
people instead of collapsing into one, and it survives the person changing their email.

Send it and `owner` together: the id is how the submitter is matched, and the address is how
they are notified, so `owner` is still required.

**Adding it later is safe.** If you have been submitting without it, the first submission that
carries an id is matched by `owner` and the id is adopted onto that existing person — your
submitters are upgraded, not duplicated. From then on the id is what identifies them.

At most 255 characters; longer returns 422 rather than being truncated, because a truncated
id would silently resolve to the wrong person. Compared exactly, including case.

issuer.description:
Which of your systems `submitterId` came from. Only meaningful alongside `submitterId`.

Send it when more than one of your systems posts to the same portal: user `42` in your billing
app is not user `42` in your analytics app, and without an issuer they would resolve to one
person. With one system you can omit it — it defaults to this portal.

The same value the browser/widget route carries as its token `iss` claim, so a submitter
resolves to the same person whichever route their feedback arrives on.

At most 255 characters; longer returns 422.

submitterName.description:
The submitter's name, as your own system holds it.

Send it and the portal shows a person. Omit it and the only name Craft can produce is the
local part of `owner`, so `jane.doe@acme.com` reads as "jane.doe" on every card and in every
digest.

**Refreshed on every submission that matches**, not only on the first one — the same as
`owner`. If the person is renamed in your system, the next submission carrying their
`submitterId` updates the stored name, so you never have to reconcile it separately.

One string, not first/last: it is split on the last space for storage and joined back for
display, so what you send is what the portal shows.

Requires pass-through identity on the portal, like `submitterId`, and requires `owner` — a
name with nobody to attach it to is a 422 rather than a value quietly dropped.

At most 256 characters; longer returns 422 rather than being truncated.

sourceUrl.description:
The page this feedback was submitted from — **including its query string.**

The query string is the point, not an incidental: a tenant, an account or a product area often
sits in a URL parameter, and a PM reading the feedback item needs the link that reproduces what
the submitter was looking at. Nothing is stripped, re-encoded or normalised.

In a single-page application send the URL **in view at submit**, not the one the page first
loaded with — they are usually different and only the first is useful.

Must be an absolute `http://` or `https://` URL of at most 2048 characters. Anything else
(a relative path, a `javascript:` or `data:` URL, surrounding whitespace, a NUL byte) returns
422 rather than being stored or quietly cleaned up.

Optional, and omitting it is the ordinary case for a backend integration that has no page.

attachmentIds.description:
Files to attach, as ids returned by `POST /feedback_portal/{portalId}/attachment`.

**Upload first, then submit.** The upload call stores the bytes against the portal and hands
back an id; naming that id here is what files it with this piece of feedback. That order is
what lets a form attach files while the submitter is still typing — there is no feedback item
to attach to until they press send — and it means a failed upload costs a retry rather than
the whole submission.

Each id must be one of **this** portal's own uploads and must not already be attached to
another feedback item; anything else is a 422. At most 10 per item. Unlike `metadata`, an id
that resolves to nothing is never quietly dropped — an attachment the submitter watched upload
must not vanish behind a 200.

metadata.description:
Context your own application wants to attach — the plan, the application version, the tenant —
keyed by **custom-field id** and mapped onto this portal's own custom fields.

**A key matching no field on the form is ignored, never a failure.** That is the whole contract:
your page's template ships on your release cycle and a PM changes the portal's fields whenever
they like, so the two WILL drift, and a stale key must never cost you a piece of feedback. The
same applies to a value the field cannot hold — dropped, not rejected. Use `customFields` when
you want an unknown id or a bad value to be a 422 instead.

**Keyed by id, not by display name**, precisely because a name is what gets renamed. Discover
ids via `GET /feedback_portal/{portalId}/widget/{widgetId}/config` or
`GET /feedback_portal/{portalId}/forms`.

**`customFields` wins.** A field named in both is taken from `customFields`, because that is
where the value the submitter could see and change arrives.

**Never identity.** The submitter's name, email and company come from the signed token (or from
`owner`/`company`) and are never read from here — an unsigned value would be a second source of
something Craft already holds signed. Since keys are custom-field ids, no key can name them.

At most 20 keys and 4 KB in total, and unlike an unknown key this **is** a 422: sending your
whole application state is a bug you hit on the first try, not drift that appears months later.

FeedbackAttachment.description: One stored file, as returned by POST /feedback_portal/{portalId}/attachment.

id.description: Pass this to `attachmentIds` on the create call.

name.description: The original file name, as uploaded.

mime.description: Detected MIME type — read from the bytes, not from the upload's Content-Type.

PortalTerminology.description:
A renamed portal term.

SHAPED LIKE `Terminology` BUT NOT THE SAME TYPE, and the missing field is the reason. Workspace
terms carry a `category` because the settings screen groups thirteen of them under four headings;
a portal has exactly two and the core has no grouping for them. Synthesising one would be a field
that can never vary and means nothing — worse than its absence, because a caller would key on it.

default.description: The untranslated term — what Craft calls it when nobody has renamed it.

customSingle.description: The administrator's word for it, or `default` when they have not chosen one.

WidgetFormField.description:
One row of a form, of either kind.

**`kind` decides where the value goes on submit**, which is why it is here rather than left to
the caller to infer from the shape of `id`. A `custom` field's value belongs in `customFields`
keyed by this `id`, a bigint the portal assigned. A `system` field's `id` is a name — Craft's own
key for a built-in part of the form, `description` being the only one the product writes today —
and its value is the request property of that name.

**`required` is a rendering instruction on a `system` field.** Nothing in Craft rejects a
submission over it, so ignoring it does not fail; it just draws a form the portal's own no longer
matches. On a `custom` field it is enforced.

The descriptive keys (`name`, `type`, `options`, …) belong to created fields and are absent on a
built-in one, which Craft holds no label or type for — the page knows how to draw its own
description box.

orderIndex.description:
The administrator's position for this field, both kinds on one scale — the array is already
sorted by it, so this is here to be read rather than acted on. Not dense and not necessarily
positive: a form nobody has re-saved since the editor gained drag ordering carries positions
the monolith's counter allocated.

description.description:
The help line drawn under the label, as the portal's own form draws it. Plain text — render it
as text, never as HTML. Absent when the field has none.

multi.description: SELECT fields only: send `values: [...]` when true, a scalar `value` when false.

WidgetForm.description:
ONE FIELD LIST, ALREADY IN RENDER ORDER — a form as the widget draws it.

The portal keeps two lists: the fields somebody created and the ones Craft builds in. Its form
editor arranges them as one, so the description box can sit between two created fields — and the
two are merged and sorted here so a page can loop over `fields` once, top to bottom, and be done.

isDefault.description: True for the portal's default form — what a category with no form of its own is given.

WidgetConfig.description:
Everything the embedded feedback widget needs to render its form, in one read.

ONE CALL AT FORM-OPEN, and the narrowing is server-side. A widget offers a chosen set of
categories, and applying that here rather than in the page is what stops a widget configured for
one category being made to render another — the browser is not a place to enforce it.

defaultImportanceId.description:
The importance to submit while `hideImportance` is true — what the administrator chose
instead of asking.

**Already resolved.** If the importance it named has since been deleted from the portal, this
is the first of `importances` rather than a dangling id, so the value is always one you can
post. Nothing is written back: the widget's stored configuration is untouched and the fallback
is worked out on every read, so restoring the importance restores the choice.

**Null means nothing was picked**, which is an ordinary state and not an error. Submit with no
`importanceId` and the portal's default applies.

Present regardless of `hideImportance` — a widget that shows the field keeps its stored value,
so an administrator toggling the question off and on again does not lose it. **When the field
is shown, this is not the value to send**: send what the submitter chose.

hideImportance.description:
True when this widget's form should not ask how important the feedback is — **leave the row
out entirely rather than showing it disabled.**

Per widget, because the judgement is per placement: a form behind a "Report a bug" button in
a product header asks somebody mid-task, who leaves whatever is preselected, so the field
costs a line and returns a value nobody chose.

**Then submit `defaultImportanceId` as the `importanceId`** — that is the administrator's
answer in place of the submitter's. When it is null, submit without an `importanceId` at all
and the feedback takes the portal's default importance (its `isDefault` one, or its first
otherwise).

title.description: The heading submitters read. Not the administrator's internal name, which is never shown.

primaryColor.description: Portal-global, not per widget. Null when the administrator has not chosen one.

terminology.description:
The portal's own words for the two things this form talks about, so the widget can label
itself the way the portal does.

`feedback` and `company`, always both, each with `default` (what Craft calls it), `customSingle`
and `customPlural` (what this portal's administrator calls it). A portal that has renamed
nothing still returns both, filled in with the defaults — the caller never has to know what
Craft would have called it.

**This is the drift argument again.** A customer's hand-built form hardcodes "Submit feedback"
and keeps saying it after a PM renamed the term to "Request"; the portal's own form cannot,
because the word arrives with the definition. Same reason the fields come from here.

forms.description:
The portal's own form definitions, narrowed to the widget's offered categories — each field
carrying whether it is required, so the widget can catch a missing one before posting rather
than by a rejection.

**Look a form up by category id.** Each offered category appears on exactly one form, so a
category is never left without one: where the portal's administrator has not given a category
a form of its own, the portal's default form (`isDefault`) covers it — and that is the same
form the submission is checked against, so a required field here is a required field there.
The one exception is a portal with no default form and no form for the category, which has no
fields to render and none to enforce.

RateLimitErrorResponse.description:
The 429 body. Its own schema for the same reason as `RetryableErrorResponse`: the rate-limit
handler emits four keys beyond `message`, and `GeneralErrorResponse` forbids all of them.

reason.description: Which bucket denied the request, for propagation to an MCP/agent caller.

WidgetEventRequest.description:
One thing the embedded widget did on a customer's page, for Craft to emit as a BI event.

**Fire and forget.** The response is `202` with no body and carries no meaning beyond "received";
ignore it, do not retry it, and never let it delay or fail a submission. Nothing here changes
anything a person can see.

**What Craft never receives through this endpoint**: the page's URL, anything the submitter typed,
their identity, and any property not listed below — an unlisted key is a `422`, so a typo is
something you find on your first attempt rather than a series that silently never arrives.
(`sourceUrl` on the create routes is how page context reaches a *submission*; this is not it.)

eventName.description:
What happened. **`beWidgetOpened`** — the form was shown to somebody. **`beWidgetSubmitted`** —
they submitted it. Anything else is a `422` listing the two.

portalId.description: Optional, and must match the portal in the path when sent. The path is what counts.

widgetId.description: Optional, and must match the widget in the path when sent.

widgetVersion.description: The widget bundle's own version, e.g. `v1`.

browser.description: The browser's user-agent string, up to 256 characters.

mobile.description: Whether it was drawn on a phone-sized screen.

categoriesSize.description: How many categories this widget offered on this open.

capacityEnabled.description:
NUMBER fields only: true when the container plans capacity against this
field. A capacity field (FE, BE) is otherwise indistinguishable from any
other number (Reach, ACV) here. Read the limits with /capacity.

description.description:
The help line the portal draws under the field's label — plain text, trimmed. Absent when the
field has none, blank included: the portal draws nothing for a blank one either.

orderIndex.description:
Position on the form. ONE SEQUENCE WITH FormSystemField.orderIndex — the form editor sends both
kinds' positions in the same save (`PortalForm::fieldsProcessing` and
`formSystemFieldsProcessing` each store what it sent), so an administrator can put the
description box between two created fields and the numbers say so.

A SORT KEY, NOT AN ORDINAL: compare two of these, don't read one on its own. A field added
without an explicit position takes the monolith's product-wide allocator
(`Item::getNexVal` — `-floor(microtime(true) * 1000)`), so a form nobody has re-saved since
carries large negative values, newest first. Dense 1..n only means the editor has saved a drag
arrangement for that form. Renumbering them here would move the description box on every widget
rendering such a form, and would disagree with the portal's own form, which sorts the raw values.

isDefault.description:
True for the portal's default form — the fields the UI shows for new feedback in a category
that has no form of its own. A portal has at most one.

fields.description: In the administrator's own order — see the ORDER BY in getPortalForms.

portal_token.description: A short-lived token signed by the customer's own server with their feedback portal's widget secret, carrying the identity of whoever is submitting. Accepted only on the two feedback-creation routes, in place of x-api-key. Used by the portal's embedded feedback widget; the customer's own integration uses x-api-key instead.

info.title: Craft.io Public API
info.description:
Our platform provides a set of comprehensive public APIs that allows users and applications to access and retrieve data about working items within our system.

With our API, users can easily integrate item information into their own applications, such as dashboards or organizational tools for customer service, sales, and marketing.

Our API supports a variety of data formats and retrieval methods, making it easy to customize and integrate with your existing systems. Whether you're looking to build custom reports, track inventory, or monitor sales trends, our API provides the flexibility and scalability you need to get the job done.

For getting an API key just approach our support team at [support@craft.io](mailto:support@craft.io) or on the app chat (‘contact support’).

post.description:
Create a feedback item without custom fields, attributed to the person who submitted it.

Identical to `POST /feedback_portal/{portalId}/feedback` except that it accepts no
`customFields`. Everything below applies to both.

**Discovering what to send.** Do not hard-code a field list. `GET /feedback_portal/{portalId}/forms`
returns each form with its categories and which fields it requires, and
`GET /feedback_portal/{portalId}/custom_fields` returns the field definitions and their allowed
values. Both are readable with any key that can read the portal, and a form definition is the
same for every visitor — so a client can render a form dynamically and never drift from what
the portal actually defines.

**Attribution.** Send `owner` (the submitter's email) and, if you have one, `submitterId` —
your own id for that person, which is the stronger key — plus `submitterName`, without which
the portal can only show the local part of the address. A submitter the portal has not seen is
created as a portal user who holds no password and can never sign in; they exist so the
feedback is attributed to a real person and so their next submission resolves to the same one.
A submission that MATCHES an existing submitter also refreshes their stored name and
notification address from what you sent, so a rename or an address change on your side needs no
separate reconciliation. Omit all of them, or send `anonymous: true`, and the item is attributed
to the portal's anonymous submitter instead. Attributed submissions require pass-through
identity to be enabled on the portal.

**Retries may duplicate the ITEM, never the person.** There is no idempotency key. If a
request times out and you re-send it, the submitter resolves to the same person — that is
guaranteed — but you may get a second feedback item, which is visible in the portal and
deletable. Guard on your own side if a duplicate item matters to you.

**Which failures to retry.** `503` means the request was fine and Craft could not complete it:
retry it. Any `4xx` means the request itself is wrong — retrying will not help, so raise it
instead. Craft never guesses that two submissions are the same one, so identical content is
never deduplicated.

**A second credential, for submitting from a browser.** This route also accepts
`Authorization: Bearer <token>` in place of `x-api-key` — a short-lived token your own server
signs with your feedback portal's widget secret (scheme `portal_token`). It exists because no
credential that reaches a browser can be kept secret, so the page carries a signed claim about
who is submitting rather than a key. On that credential the identity is taken from the token's
claims (`sub`, `email`, `name`, `company`, `iss`) and `owner`, `submitterId`, `issuer`,
`submitterName`, `anonymous` and `company` in the BODY are rejected with 422 — the page is
under the submitter's control and the token is not. The token is good for one hour from `iat`
whatever its `exp` says, covers as many submissions as the person makes inside that hour, and
is not single use. A `401` with `error: "token_expired"` means fetch a new one and retry;
`error: "token_invalid"` will never succeed on retry.

**Before you build the signing half**, a portal can issue a *development* key
(`Authorization: Bearer cwk_dev_…`) which is sent as-is with the identity fields in the body,
accepted only from an origin the administrator registered as development. Everything it creates
is marked as development in the portal's user list. It is a different key from the production
one, so what you paste into a page while building can never sign a real submission.

**What to send, and how to know it is right.** `GET /feedback_portal/{portalId}/widget/{widgetId}/config`
returns the widget's categories and the portal's own fields with their `required` flags, so a
form can be rendered from the portal's definition and a missing field caught before posting
rather than by a rejection here.

**A stale `importanceId` does not cost you the submission.** On either widget credential, an
importance id the portal no longer has — an administrator can delete one while your page is
open — is dropped and the portal's default applied, rather than refused. On `x-api-key` it is
a 422 listing the valid ids, because that caller can re-read them and retry.

**No cookie is set and no Craft session exists**, on this call or on the config read. Worth
stating as a property rather than an implementation detail: nothing about the person submitting
is stored in their browser by Craft, which is usually the question a customer's privacy review
asks first.

post.description:
Upload a file so it can be attached to a piece of feedback.

**Upload first, then submit.** `multipart/form-data` with the file in a field named `file`. The
response carries an `id`; pass it in `attachmentIds` on
`POST /feedback_portal/{portalId}/feedback` or `.../plain_feedback` to file it with that
submission. Call this once per file.

That order is not a preference. A form's file picker fires while the person is still writing,
so there is no feedback item to attach to yet — and it means a failed upload costs a retry of
one file rather than the whole submission.

**Until a create call names it, the file belongs to the portal and to nothing else.** It is not
visible on any feedback item, and an id from a different portal is refused.

**Limits.** 20 MB per file, 10 files per feedback item. Executable and script types are refused
(422 `file_type_not_allowed`), as is a file whose bytes do not match an image extension it
claims (422 `file_content_mismatch`). Over the size cap is 413 `file_too_large`. Files are
virus-scanned after this call returns; an infected file is removed along with its links.

**Reading attachments back is not part of this release** — this endpoint stores them; the
portal and the Craft app display them.

Takes the same three credentials as the create routes: an account API key, a widget token, or a
development key.

get.description:
Everything the portal's embedded feedback widget needs to render its form, in one read.

**Called when the form opens, not when the page loads.** The widget fetches its signed token
from your own server at that moment and uses it here, which is why an hour-long token is
comfortable: the window only has to cover somebody writing, not their whole visit.

**The fields come from the portal every time.** A PM adding a required field appears in the
widget on the next page load with nobody editing your site — which is the point of embedding
the portal's own form rather than a copy of it. Each field carries `required`, so the widget can
catch a missing one before posting instead of by a rejection.

**Read this when the widget OPENS, not when the page loads.** Everything here is a setting an
administrator can change at any moment, so the response is `Cache-Control: no-store` and a copy
held across a long-lived page goes out of date. Nothing can make this read and the submission
that follows one transaction, which is why a stale `importanceId` is forgiven on submit rather
than refused — but the fresher this read, the less often a submitter is shown an option that
has since gone.

**One list, already in order.** A form's built-in fields — its description box — are the
portal's to show, hide, reorder and mark required, exactly like a field somebody created, so a
page that hardcodes them drifts the moment an administrator changes their mind. Both kinds
arrive merged in `fields`, sorted the way the form editor arranges them — the description box
can sit between two created fields, and it will here too. Draw the array top to bottom.

Each entry carries `kind`, which is also where its value goes on submit: a `custom` field's
belongs in `customFields` under its id, a `system` field's is the request property its `id`
names.

**The categories are the widget's, narrowed here.** A widget offers a chosen set; that
narrowing is applied server-side, so what comes back is exactly what the form may show. Every
offered category is covered by exactly one form: a category with no form of its own gets the
portal's default form, which is the same form the submission will be validated against.

**`widget.hideImportance` means leave the row out, not disable it.** Draw no importance control
at all, and post `widget.defaultImportanceId` as the `importanceId` — that is the answer the
administrator gave in place of the submitter's, which is the point of hiding the question rather
than a detail of it. A null there means nobody picked one: post no `importanceId` and the
portal's default applies.

**`defaultImportanceId` is already resolved.** An administrator deleting the importance a widget
named does not break it and does not rewrite it: the fallback to the first of `importances` is
worked out on every read and nothing is written back, so restoring the importance restores the
choice.

**So do the words.** `terminology` carries the portal's own names for feedback and for a
company — `{ default, customSingle, customPlural }` for each, always both keys, defaults filled
in when nobody has renamed anything. A portal that calls feedback a "Request" gets a form that
says Request, for the same reason it gets the portal's fields: a copy of the form hardcodes the
word and keeps saying it after a PM changes it.

**No cookie is set and no Craft session exists** — on this call or on the submission that
follows it. That is a property of the feature rather than an implementation detail: nothing
about the person browsing your site is stored in their browser by Craft.

post.description:
Tell Craft that the widget was opened, or submitted, on your page.

**Fire and forget.** `202` with no body, and the body means nothing beyond "received". Do not
retry it, do not wait for it before showing your form, and never let it fail a submission — a
relay that breaks the thing it measures is worse than no measurement.

**What to send.** `eventName` is `beWidgetOpened` (the form was shown to somebody) or
`beWidgetSubmitted`. Everything else is optional context about the page:

```json
{ "eventName": "beWidgetOpened", "widgetVersion": "v1",
  "browser": "<navigator.userAgent>", "mobile": false, "categoriesSize": 3 }
```

`portalId` and `widgetId` may also be sent and must then match the path, which is what counts.

**Nothing about the person reaches Craft through this endpoint** — no page URL, nothing typed
into the form, no identity. An unlisted property is a `422` rather than a silent drop, so a typo
is something you see on your first attempt instead of a series that never arrives.

Takes the same three credentials as the config read: a widget token, a development key, or an
account API key.
